extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemakers, federal permitting agencies, state and tribal certifying authorities, and environmental law practitioners/advocates
extracted.subtask_description: A public legal comment/advocacy brief critiquing EPA's proposed revisions to Clean Water Act §401, arguing for specific statutory interpretations, procedural protections, and minimum application requirements that preserve state/tribal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'applicant' under §401(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'applicant' in section 401(d) should be interpreted as identifying the person or entity responsible for obtaining and complying with the certification; this term is plain and unambiguous and EPA must give effect to Congress's choice of words rather than read them coextensively with 'discharge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must explain how interpreting 'applicant' differently leads to limiting 401(d) to conditions only on an applicant's discharges; reaffirming existing understanding of which actor is subject to limits under 401(d) offers no basis for narrowing the actions that may be limited. EPA's interpretation must give effect to Congress's use of different terms (e.g., 'discharge' vs. 'applicant') and cannot ignore that difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'other appropriate requirement of state law'
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's reading that this phrase covers only EPA‑approved CWA regulatory programs that control discharges is too narrow; states retain authority (via references to sections 301 and 303) to impose broader, non-discharge-based limits (e.g., in‑stream flow conditions) necessary to protect water quality standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if 'other appropriate requirement' were read to mean EPA‑approved programs, Section 401's cross‑references (to §301 and §303) independently permit states to impose conditions on non‑discharge activities. EPA's asserted authority to cabin this phrase does not support an overall limitation of §401(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on relying on Brand X to overturn prior interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cannot invoke Brand X deference to reject PUD No. 1 unless Brand X's narrow criteria are met — namely that a prior court's interpretation involved choosing among reasonable constructions of ambiguous text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PUD No. 1 was effectively a Chevron step 1/plain‑meaning case, not an ambiguous‑text case choosing among reasonable interpretations; EPA must demonstrate ambiguity and that its interpretation is reasonable before using Brand X or agency deference to displace that precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of environmental consequences of narrowing §401(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must acknowledge and justify environmental consequences of any narrow interpretation of §401(d) that would preclude states from imposing non‑discharge conditions; many activities requiring §401 certification have serious non‑discharge water quality impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comment lists impacts that states may address under §401: increases in sediment loads; reduced stream flows; thermal loading from removal of riparian vegetation; destabilized stream banks; altered groundwater regimes; designation of waters as 'waste treatment systems'; acid mine drainage/metals leaching; and perpetual water treatment obligations. EPA must show how prohibition of conditions addressing these harms would still 'assur[e] that Federal licensing or permitting agencies cannot override State water quality requirements.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/scope of 'discharge' under §401
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'discharge' is not limited to point sources; the Supreme Court defined it as a 'flowing or issuing out' and Congress elsewhere distinguished 'discharge' from 'discharge of a pollutant' (the latter defined with reference to point sources), so §401's unqualified use of 'discharge' should be read broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory‑construction principles (Russello/Barnhart/Conn. Nat’l Bank) counsel against importing 'point source' limitations into 'discharge' where Congress chose not to include them. Circuit precedent and the structure of the CWA support a broader meaning that can include nonpoint impacts; EPA may not add qualifying language Congress omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for certification denials
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 401(a)(1) makes state certification contingent on an affirmative showing that 'any such discharge will comply' with applicable provisions, placing the burden on the applicant; proposed §121.5(e) improperly would require states to identify requirements the project 'will not comply' with, effectively shifting the burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed §121.5(e) should be revised to require a state to identify 'the specific water quality requirements that the state cannot confirm the proposed project will comply with' and to state why the state cannot confirm compliance. A state may deny when it cannot affirmatively conclude compliance; the rule must not force the state to prove a violation to deny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of denials based on uncertainty and residual risk
rubrics_metrics.description: States must be permitted to deny a certification when residual risks from a project are unacceptably likely to cause violations, even if a violation cannot be proven certain to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state should explain the risks of concern and how potential incidents (e.g., frac‑outs, tailings dam failures) would violate water requirements. Requiring certainty of a violation to deny would violate the precautionary spirit and text of §401(a)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on federal agencies reviewing the substance of state/tribal §401 decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal permitting agencies lack statutory authority to review or overrule the substance of state or tribal denials or conditions under §401; both §401(a)(1) and §401(d) give states the last word and contain no text authorizing federal substantive review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's proposed provisions (§121.6(c)(2), §121.8(a)(2)) that would let federal agencies treat state denials as waivers or convert conditional certifications to unconditional ones are unlawful. Every circuit to consider the issue has held federal permitting agencies lack this substantive review authority; Congress deliberately assigned decisionmaking to states and provided judicial review as the remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between procedural and substantive review
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies may have limited authority to verify state compliance with §401's procedural requirements (e.g., public notice), but they may not evaluate or replace the substantive determinations a state makes about water quality or impose additional legal requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases permitting narrow procedural verification (City of Tacoma, etc.) expressly caution against 'second guessing' or resolving disputes that require construing state law. Federal agencies cannot add procedural or substantive requirements beyond what the statute contemplates (e.g., impose claim‑preclusion rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review as the appropriate remedy for disputing state §401 decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a party disputes the validity of a state or tribal denial or condition under §401, judicial review is the established and appropriate remedy; EPA has not shown that judicial review is inadequate to protect interests or that federal agency review is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have authority to overturn 'invalid' state decisions and to remand for further state consideration; judicial review also provides standards and recourse (including opportunities to revise decisions) that EPA's proposed administrative review lacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'water quality requirements' under §401
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's attempt to define 'water quality requirements' narrowly (to effluent limits, WQS, national performance standards, and EPA‑approved state/tribal CWA regulatory program provisions) is inconsistent with the statute and congressional intent to give states/tribes broad authority under §401.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Congress had intended an enumerated list, it would have done so as elsewhere in §1341(a)(1). The legislative history cited by EPA does not support limiting §401 to EPA‑approved requirements. Examples EPA cites of allegedly unrelated conditions (trails, payments, public access) lack context and may be directly related to water quality in ways EPA ignores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of a 'valid' certification request (what triggers the §401 clock)
rubrics_metrics.description: The one‑year 'reasonable time' clock under §401 should begin only upon receipt of a 'valid' certification request that contains minimum, project‑specific information sufficient for the state/tribe to begin meaningful review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's proposed document list is inadequate. At minimum a valid request should include: (a) designation of all waterways that could be affected, including whether impaired and what standards are not met and whether waterways are high/exceptional quality; (b) detailed description of the 'type' of discharge (chemical composition, thermal/nonchemical discharges, source of discharge, estimated volume); (c) identification of the number of discharges per waterway/watershed and estimated date for applicant's analysis of direct/indirect/cumulative impacts; (d) identification of any other impacts to water quality; (e) an estimated date when applicant will provide a complete, site‑specific mitigation plan; (f) payment of applicable fees as part of the request; (g) existing documentation or a statement about prior contamination; (h) a process for the state/tribe to inform the relevant federal agency that an initial submission is not a valid request; and (i) a certification that the proponent notified the relevant federal agency the same day as sending the request to the state/tribe, including method of transmission and contact person.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA should not force a single standardized form for all projects
rubrics_metrics.description: A single, one‑size‑fits‑all form is insufficient to capture the variable, project‑specific data states and tribes need to evaluate §401 impacts across diverse projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because project information needs vary widely (e.g., pipelines crossing many streams vs. single‑site projects), EPA should not adopt a mandatory universal form that could allow federal agencies to accept less information than states require; AES Sparrows Point and other cases support conditioning the clock on a valid request tailored to the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 401 'reasonable time' and federal agency deadline limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional 'reasonable time (not to exceed one year)' prevents unreasonable delay but does not empower federal agencies to set arbitrary or prematurely short deadlines that would make certification impossible or force premature denials/waivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal agencies may adopt regulations about what constitutes a reasonable time, but may not exercise that authority in a way that deprives states/tribes of their substantive §401 authority. A federal agency finding of waiver should not be used to curtail state/tribal ability to evaluate complex projects; deadlines must reflect project complexity and information flows (iterative applicant‑state processes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal agencies cannot prematurely find waiver in order to limit state/tribal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Although federal agencies can determine whether a waiver has occurred, they cannot set timelines or employ waiver findings in ways that prevent states/tribes from exercising their substantive certification authority under §401.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's proposed scheme for increased federal involvement in setting 'reasonable time' is divorced from the realities of complex projects and risks forcing premature denials; courts (Millennium Pipeline, City of Tacoma) limit federal authority and emphasize deference to states on substantive issues.
